findings.title: Do not pipe unpinned remote script into sh at build time
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` fetches code over the network and executes it as root during the image build with no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and no TLS-identity pinning. The build output is non-reproducible and any compromise of the remote host, DNS, or a MITM yields arbitrary code execution baked into the image. The URL also points at the reserved placeholder domain `example.com`, so the fetched body is not a real installer — the line either fails or executes unrelated content.

findings.title: Pipeline masks curl failure so build silently succeeds
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN` executes through `/bin/sh -c`; without `set -o pipefail` the pipeline's exit status is `sh`'s, not `curl`'s. `curl` is also missing `-f`, so HTTP error bodies are fed to `sh` as script text. On a network/DNS failure curl exits non-zero while `sh` reads empty stdin and exits 0, so the layer reports success and the image ships without the tool the install script was supposed to provide. Failure is no longer distinguishable from a legitimate successful install, and the failure only surfaces later at container runtime.

findings.title: Do not curl|sh an unpinned, unverified remote script in build
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes arbitrary code fetched over the network as root during image build with no version pin, checksum, or signature. The content at that URL can change at any time (or be substituted by a MITM/compromised host/DNS), and every build/reproduce/cache-miss will run whatever is served, so the image is not reproducible and can be trojaned without any repo change.

findings.title: Download failure is swallowed: build succeeds with no install
findings.whyItBreaks: The RUN is a shell pipeline `curl ... | sh`. The pipeline's exit status is the last command's (`sh`), and `curl` runs without `-f`, so HTTP 4xx/5xx (e.g. a 404 or moved URL) and `-s`-silenced network errors do not fail the RUN. `sh` reads an empty/error body, exits 0, and the layer is cached as successful — producing an image that silently lacks whatever the script was meant to install. Failure and success are indistinguishable in the build result.

findings.title: Pin and verify remote install script instead of curl|sh
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes arbitrary remote code as root during the image build with no integrity check (no checksum, signature, or pinned version). Anyone who controls example.com (or the network/DNS/TLS path) at build time gains code execution in the resulting image, and the build is non-reproducible because the fetched content can change silently. `-s` also suppresses curl's error output and there is no `-f`/`--fail`, so an HTTP error (404/5xx) still exits 0 and pipes the error-page body into `sh`, hiding a failed download.

findings.title: Stop discarding ErrMissing in exported LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load (src/store.go:7-13) returns ErrMissing when the key is absent, and also returns "" (nil error) when the key is present with an empty value. LoadOrDefault discards the error via `v, _ := Load(key, m)` (src/store.go:16), so the exported API cannot distinguish "key absent" from "key present but empty" — both surface as "". Any caller that needs to treat a missing key differently from an empty one (presence checks, defaults that differ from "", validation) is forced to act on the fallback as if it were real data, with no way to detect the failure.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing, conflating missing with empty
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault is an exported (public) helper whose body does `v, _ := Load(key, m)` at src/store.go:16, discarding the ErrMissing signal that Load returns at src/store.go:10. On a missing key it returns "", which is byte-for-byte identical to the value Load returns for a key that exists and legitimately holds an empty string. Because the function takes no default argument and does not log or wrap the error, every caller is forced to conflate "absent" with "present-but-empty" — the package already provides Load precisely so callers can distinguish these, and this new public path erases that distinction with no way to recover it at the call site.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing, conflating failure with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault (exported, package store) ignores the error from Load via `v, _ :=`. Load returns ErrMissing only when the key is absent; a key that IS present with value "" returns ("", nil). Both cases now yield "", so every caller is forced to conflate "key missing" (Load previously signalled this to callers at src/store.go:10) with "key present and legitimately empty". This is a present API-contract defect regardless of whether any in-repo caller exists yet: a caller that treats the returned string as real persisted data (e.g. writes it back, reports it as configured, uses it for routing/validation) cannot detect the missing-key case and will act on the fallback as if it were real.

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines finish; result sends are unsupervised
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously each `results <- j * 2` completed before Run returned, so a caller could safely treat Run's return as 'all results delivered' (e.g. close(results), or proceed to consume). The new loop spawns one goroutine per job and Run returns immediately with no WaitGroup, no completion channel, and no close. A caller that closes results right after Run returns now races the goroutine sends and panics with `send on closed channel`; a caller that stops receiving leaves every spawned goroutine blocked forever on the unbuffered send (goroutine leak). There is no longer any way for a caller to know when the work is done.

findings.title: Run no longer waits for work; unbounded goroutines + lost completion
findings.whyItBreaks: Base Run sent every result on the caller's goroutine, so it only returned after all jobs were enqueued — a caller could safely `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` or assume work was done on return. The new body launches a goroutine per job and returns immediately. Any caller that closes `results` right after Run returns now races the still-running goroutines and panics with 'send on closed channel'; a caller that exits early (error path, ctx cancel, deadline) leaves every spawned goroutine permanently blocked on `results <-`, leaking N goroutines. Parallelism is also unbounded (one goroutine per element of `jobs`), so a large `jobs` slice fans out without limit, and result ordering is no longer deterministic. The signature/doc are unchanged, so the public contract still implies the old synchronous behavior.

findings.title: Run now returns before any result is sent, breaking its completion contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change each `results <- j*2` was a blocking send executed inline, so `Run` returned only after all len(jobs) results had been delivered, in jobs order. Now every send runs in a detached goroutine and `Run` returns immediately after the loop. The idiomatic caller `worker.Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` now panics with `send on closed channel` as soon as a spawned goroutine sends after the close, and a caller that inspects results right after `Run` returns can observe an incomplete/empty set. Ordering is also no longer deterministic: results[i] no longer corresponds to jobs[i], so index-based consumers mis-associate values. Because the sends are no longer sequenced, no completion signal (WaitGroup/close) replaces the removed guarantee.

findings.title: Unbounded goroutines block on send and leak when results is not drained
findings.whyItBreaks: The loop spawns one goroutine per job with no bound and no cancellation. If `results` is unbuffered, the receiver stops early, or `ctx` is cancelled, each spawned goroutine blocks forever on `results <- j*2` because nothing selects on ctx.Done() and nothing closes the channel; the old inline send instead applied backpressure to the caller and could not leak. With a large `jobs` slice this also creates len(jobs) concurrent goroutines at once, whereas the prior code used a single sender. The unused `ctx` parameter means cancellation cannot interrupt a blocked send.

findings.title: Log's new tag parameter is ignored, silently dropping caller tags
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature `func Log(message string, tag ...string)` promises callers that the supplied tag values participate in logging, but the body `println(message)` never reads `tag`. Any caller that passes tags (e.g. `Log("x", "auth")`) receives output identical to passing none, so the tagging contract is silently unmet and the extra arguments are dropped without warning. This is an exported/public carrier, so the promise is the contract.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord OR flips to over-permissive delete authorization
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate changed from `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` to `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId`. Under the new logic a non-admin user sharing a tenant with a record now passes the gate (privilege escalation: any same-tenant user can delete records they previously could not), and an admin in tenant A now passes for a record owned by tenant B (tenant isolation bypass / cross-tenant data loss). This exported authorization predicate is the public contract for the delete decision, so it is a defect even with no in-repo callers: every caller is forced to trust a gate that authorizes deletions it must not.

findings.title: Widened delete permission: OR replaces AND in canDeleteRecord
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` to `||` inverts the policy in two ways. (1) In-tenant privilege escalation: `session.tenantId === record.tenantId` alone now short-circuits true, so any non-admin user can delete any record in their tenant, including records they do not own (record.ownerId is ignored). (2) Cross-tenant deletion: `session.isAdmin` alone now short-circuits true, so an admin of tenant A can delete records belonging to tenant B, bypassing tenant isolation. Both are destructive, unauthorized actions that the pre-change guard rejected.

findings.title: Fix canDeleteRecord: OR lets non-admins and cross-tenant admins delete
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate changed from `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` to `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId`. Deletion authorization previously required BOTH admin role AND tenant match; the OR now grants delete when EITHER holds. This produces two concrete authorization bypasses: (1) a non-admin user whose tenantId equals record.tenantId (e.g. an ordinary member of the tenant) now passes and can delete records they were never authorized to delete; (2) an admin from any other tenant now passes regardless of record.tenantId, defeating cross-tenant isolation. Both are the exact cases the original AND existed to block, so this is an under-blocking authorization regression, not a tightening.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows errors and silently resets settings to defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously JSON.parse / validation failures threw, so a corrupt or partial raw string never produced a settings object. Now the catch returns a fresh DEFAULTS copy, conflating failure with a legitimate value. updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20) consumes that fallback, mutates fontSize, and unconditionally persists it via save (src/settings.ts:22) — discarding the user's actual theme and any other stored fields. A malformed/older settings blob therefore silently resets the user to theme "light" and writes that back, with no error reaching the caller.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows parse/validation errors and returns defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously parseSettings threw on malformed JSON, a non-string theme, or a non-number fontSize, and that error propagated to callers. The new catch-all returns `{ ...DEFAULTS }` (theme "light", fontSize 14), making failure indistinguishable from a legitimately parsed value. Its caller `updateFontSize` (src/settings.ts:20) reads the result, mutates `settings.fontSize`, and persists it via `save(JSON.stringify(settings))`. Concretely: for raw `{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"big"}` the old code threw (no write, file preserved); the new code returns defaults, and updateFontSize writes `{"theme":"light","fontSize":size}` to disk, silently destroying the valid user theme. The exported function's contract is now unusable: every caller is forced to conflate a corrupt/failed parse with real settings.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows invalid-input errors and returns defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, malformed JSON / non-string theme / non-number fontSize threw and the error propagated out of parseSettings (and out of updateFontSize before save ran). Now the catch-all returns `{ ...DEFAULTS }`, so every caller is forced to conflate "parse failed" with a legitimate default settings value. The in-repo caller updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20) cannot tell the two apart: on corrupt raw it now calls save(JSON.stringify(defaults + new size)), silently overwriting the user's (possibly recoverable) settings file with defaults and losing data instead of surfacing the failure. As an exported symbol the unusable contract is itself the defect regardless of callers.

findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount is an exported public API whose name/semantics promise the number of pages needed to hold all totalItems. Any caller paginating by this count silently drops the tail items whenever totalItems % pageSize !== 0 (also returns 0 for 0 < totalItems < pageSize, e.g. 2 items/pageSize 10 -> 0 pages).

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the requested commit, not a hardcoded ref
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport(build, branch) derives `commit` from the caller-supplied `branch` (line 12) and reports it as `builtFrom`, but the artifacts are now fetched from a fixed `build.ref("verified")` (line 13) instead of `commit` (line 14). For any branch whose tip is not the "verified" ref, the returned BuildReport pairs `builtFrom` (the requested branch commit) with `artifacts` from a different commit, so callers get a self-inconsistent report and list the wrong artifacts. The `branch` parameter now silently stops governing half of the result. Additionally, the new `build.ref("verified")` lookup runs on every call and can fail (throw or resolve to a missing/empty ref) for builds that have no "verified" ref, where the previous branch lookup succeeded.

findings.title: Report mixes builtFrom branch commit with artifacts from hardcoded "verified" ref
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport(build, branch) still sets builtFrom to the commit resolved from the caller-supplied `branch`, but now fetches artifacts via build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")) from a different, hardcoded ref. The returned BuildReport therefore labels artifacts as belonging to `builtFrom` while they actually come from the "verified" revision. Any consumer reading builtFrom and artifacts together (or any branch whose "verified" ref resolves to a different/absent revision) silently gets the wrong artifact set for the reported build, and the `branch` argument no longer determines what artifacts are listed.

findings.title: Report pairs builtFrom commit with artifacts from unrelated ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change both builtFrom and artifacts came from the same resolved commit (build.ref(branch)), so the report was internally consistent. Now `artifacts` is fetched from build.ref("verified") while `builtFrom` still reports the branch commit. Whenever the "verified" ref resolves to a different commit than `branch` (the normal case: a branch tip vs. a verification tag/ref), the returned BuildReport lists artifacts that do not belong to the commit named in builtFrom, silently misrepresenting which build produced those artifacts to every consumer of this exported function.

findings.title: Restore limit slicing in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc contract at src/feed.ts:1 promises "at most `limit` entries" and the previous body enforced it with `.slice(0, limit)`. The new body drops that slice and returns the whole reversed array, so the `limit` argument is ignored for every positive value. The sole caller `renderFeed` (src/feed.ts:9) calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and then copies `page.length` entries into `new Array(20)` (src/feed.ts:10-11); assigning out[i] beyond index 19 extends the array, so renderFeed returns all entries instead of at most 20 — an unbounded feed with no cap.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit and returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc contract (line 1) promises 'at most `limit` entries', but the `.slice(0, limit)` was replaced by `if (limit <= 0) return []` followed by `return sorted`, which returns the entire reversed array whenever limit > 0. Caller renderFeed (line 9) calls recentEntries(all, 20) and then copies i < page.length entries into a size-20 array, so with more than 20 inputs it grows past 20 and returns the whole feed — a user-facing regression from the previous capped behavior.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit, returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`. The new body reverses, then returns `sorted` unconditionally for every limit > 0, so the `limit` cap is no longer applied. The only in-repo caller, renderFeed, calls recentEntries(all, 20) and copies `page.length` entries into a 20-slot array (src/feed.ts:9-12); with more than 20 inputs, `out` grows past 20 and the feed returns an unbounded page instead of the documented at-most-20. Precondition substitution: limit=20 -> `20 <= 0` is false -> returns all N entries; for all=['a'..'z'] the caller gets 26 entries instead of 20. The doc comment on line 1 still promises 'at most `limit` entries', so the carrier/body contract is also broken.

findings.title: entry-count header no longer matches emitted rows after stale filter
findings.whyItBreaks: The new filter drops stale entries from `rows` (line 20-21), but the header still receives `entries.length` (line 22), i.e. the pre-filter total. The produced manifest therefore advertises `# entry-count: N` where N includes stale entries while only `live.length` data rows follow. Any consumer that trusts `entry-count` to size or iterate the row block over-reads past the row list (or miscounts), a behavior that did not exist before this change when count always equaled the row count.

findings.title: Fix entry-count header to match filtered manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: This change filters `stale` entries out of the rendered rows (`live.map(...)` @src/manifest.ts:21) but the emitted header still passes the unfiltered `entries.length` (`headerLines(opts, entries.length)` @src/manifest.ts:22). The output therefore advertises `# entry-count: N` (all entries, including stale) while containing only the non-stale rows. Any consumer that trusts `entry-count` to size, validate, or detect truncation of the manifest (e.g. asserting `N` data lines follow the header) now sees a count larger than the actual row set, i.e. the count is silently wrong for the filtered manifest. TRIGGER C (contract drift): carrier `# entry-count:` @src/manifest.ts:15 promises the number of entries in the manifest; body now emits `entries.length` unfiltered @src/manifest.ts:22 against `live` rows @src/manifest.ts:21. `renderManifest` is exported, so this emitted header is a public contract on the function's return value.

findings.title: Manifest entry-count header counts stale entries it no longer lists
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff adds `const live = entries.filter((e) => !e.stale)` and renders only `live` rows, but the unchanged header line still calls `headerLines(opts, entries.length)`. The emitted `# entry-count: N` therefore equals the pre-filter total, while the body contains only `live.length` rows. For `[{stale:false},{stale:true}]` the output is `# entry-count: 2` followed by a single row. Any consumer that parses `entry-count` to size, verify, or detect truncation of the listing now sees a permanent mismatch: the count exceeds the rows by the number of stale entries. Because `renderManifest` is exported and its string output is the public contract, this inconsistency ships as a wrong advertised count even with no in-repo caller.

findings.title: execute() always throws, replacing its working string result
findings.whyItBreaks: `execute` is the package's only exported symbol and previously returned a deterministic value (`input.toUpperCase()`). The new body throws `new Error("always fails")` on every call, so any consumer of this public API now gets an exception instead of a result — the core (and only) path is unusable. The unchanged `: string` return type still promises a string, but no input can ever produce one.

findings.title: Restore execute(): unconditional throw breaks exported string contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Base returned `input.toUpperCase()`; head replaces the body with `throw new Error("always fails")`. The exported function is annotated `: string` and is the module's only public API, so every call now throws instead of returning a value, converting a pure success path into guaranteed failure for all consumers.

findings.title: execute() always throws, breaking its exported string contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function execute(input: string): string promises a string result (src/runner.ts:1), but the body now unconditionally throws. Any caller of this public symbol receives an exception instead of a value, so the module's only exported behavior is now unusable. The `input` parameter is also silently ignored. No in-repo caller exists, so the defect is the public contract itself: every external consumer is forced onto a path that can never succeed.

findings.title: Viewer gate in isEligible blocks the read-only route it should not govern
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() (src/handler.ts:23-28) treats viewers as a distinct, legitimate outcome: after the isEligible check it has an explicit `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";` branch (line 25). By adding `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` to isEligible, every viewer now fails isEligible and short-circuits at line 24 to "rejected", making the line-25 "read-only" branch dead code. An active viewer (e.g. {status:"active", role:"viewer", attempts:0}) previously returned "read-only" and now returns "rejected" — a real behavior regression, since viewer routing is handle()'s concern, not eligibility's.

findings.title: Viewer rejection in isEligible makes read-only path unreachable
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR a viewer request with status==="active" and attempts<MAX_ATTEMPTS passed isEligible and was served the dedicated "read-only" outcome at line 25. The added guard `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` now makes isEligible return false for every viewer, so handle() short-circuits to "rejected" at line 24 and line 25 is dead code. Every viewer loses read-only access — a user-facing behavior regression, and the still-present read-only branch proves the rejection contradicts intended behavior.

findings.title: Remove viewer check from isEligible; it over-blocks the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible now returns false for any req.role === "viewer", but handle() is the only reader of isEligible and it deliberately serves viewers via a dedicated branch: `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";` (src/handler.ts:25). Because handle() returns "rejected" at src/handler.ts:24 before reaching line 25, that branch is now dead and every active viewer request yields "rejected" instead of "read-only". At base (d996d31:src/handler.ts:20) an active viewer with attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS returned "read-only", so this is a user-facing regression. isEligible's concern is status/attempt budget; viewer role is separately governed by handle, so this predicate does not legitimately govern the read-only action.

findings.title: canProceed over-blocks saveDraft for unpaid orders
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared predicate read by two distinct actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). The change makes canProceed return false for any order whose payment is 'missing' (state 'draft' + payment 'missing' => false, since state !== 'ready' is true but payment === 'paid' is false). saveDraft does not legitimately require payment — saving a draft with a missing payment was allowed before this diff (base canProceed returned true for {state:'draft',payment:'missing'}) and now returns 'blocked' at src/actions.ts:9, a user-facing regression on a legitimately-approvable action.

findings.title: canProceed payment gate over-blocks saveDraft for unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared predicate read by two distinct actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Adding `&& order.payment === "paid"` legitimately governs submit, but saveDraft does not depend on payment. Substituting a real value: state="draft", payment="missing" → canProceed returns false → saveDraft returns "blocked" instead of "saved" (base behavior returned "saved" since state !== "ready"). Saving a draft is legitimately approvable independent of payment, so this change rejects a valid action.

findings.title: saveDraft now blocked for unpaid drafts by payment check
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed was changed from `order.state !== "ready"` to `order.state !== "ready" && order.payment === "paid"`. canProceed is a SHARED predicate read by two distinct actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). The payment precondition legitimately governs submitOrder, but it does NOT govern saveDraft. Substituting a normal draft (state="draft", payment="missing"): base returned true so saveDraft returned "saved"; head returns false (state check passes but payment==="paid" is false), so saveDraft returns "blocked". Saving a draft is legitimately approvable on its own (drafts are by definition not yet paid), so this change rejects a valid action — a user-facing workflow regression on every unpaid draft.

findings.title: publishSnapshot returns files from "stable" but reports channel head commit
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the snapshot was self-consistent: `commit: head` (headCommit(channel), src/publish.ts:13) paired with `files: repo.filesAt(head)`. The diff adds `const stable = repo.headCommit("stable")` (src/publish.ts:14) and passes `stable` to `filesAt` (src/publish.ts:18), while `commit` still reports the requested channel's head (src/publish.ts:16) and `channel` still reports the argument (src/publish.ts:17). The result is a Snapshot whose `files` belong to the "stable" commit but whose `commit`/`channel` describe a different commit. Any consumer that publishes/archives `commit` together with `files` (the whole point of the struct) ships the wrong file set for the stated commit, and `publishSnapshot(repo, "feature-x")` now silently returns stable's files regardless of the requested channel — a regression from the previous channel-correct behavior. The hardcoded "stable" also makes the `channel` parameter ineffective for file selection.

findings.title: publishSnapshot returns files from 'stable' head but reports requested channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: `commit` is set to `head` = repo.headCommit(channel) (line 13/16), but `files` is now repo.filesAt(stable) where `stable` = repo.headCommit("stable") (lines 14/18). For any channel other than "stable" (e.g. "main"), the returned Snapshot pairs a commit from one channel with the file list of a different commit, so consumers that reconstruct/serve the snapshot from `commit` will get a file list that does not correspond to that commit — silently wrong content with no error. Previously files were taken from `head` (repo.filesAt(head)), so this is a behavior regression introduced by the changed line.

findings.title: Snapshot files come from 'stable' while commit is requested channel

Now two concurrent reserve() calls for the same sku both read the same `remaining` (e.g. 1), both pass the `remaining <= 0` guard (line 16), both persist `remaining - 1`, and both return true — two successful reservations from one unit (lost update / oversell). findings.title: Invert TTL comparison: fresh entries evicted, expired entries served
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate was flipped from `< this.ttlMs` to `> this.ttlMs`. Now `get` returns the value only when the entry is OLDER than the TTL (stale data is served) and, for any entry within the TTL, falls through to `this.entries.delete(key)` and returns null. findings.title: pruneDone skips consecutive done jobs and mutates caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `forEach` with `splice` while iterating shifts indices: after removing element at `index`, the element that slides into that slot is skipped by the incrementing `forEach` cursor, so adjacent done jobs survive (e.g. [done,done,open] returns [done,open] instead of [open]). Additionally `splice` mutates the caller's array in place and the same reference is returned, whereas the prior `filter` implementation returned a new array and left the input untouched — callers holding the original array now silently observe removed jobs.

findings.title: TtlCache.get returns expired values and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The TTL guard was flipped from `<` to `>`. For a fresh entry (Date.now() - storedAt < ttlMs) the new condition is false, so the entry is deleted and get() returns null; for an expired entry (elapsed > ttlMs) the condition is true, so the stale value is returned. This inverts the cache contract: every read either misses a live entry or serves expired data that the previous code evicted.

findings.title: pruneDone mutates caller array and skips done jobs after splice

findings.title: TtlCache.get returns expired entries and drops fresh ones

Now when elapsed = Date.now() - entry.storedAt is GREATER than ttlMs (entry expired) the method returns entry.value as if valid; when elapsed is less than ttlMs (entry still fresh) it deletes the entry and returns null. This inverts the cache contract: callers receive stale/expired data and freshly stored values are immediately evicted, so the cache returns wrong values and never actually caches.

findings.title: pruneDone splice-while-iterating skips consecutive done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach advances the index by one each step while splice removes the current element and shifts the remainder left. After removing index i, the element that was at i+1 moves into slot i and is never visited. For [done, done, notDone] the result is [done, notDone] — a done job survives pruning, so callers relying on pruneDone to remove all completed jobs get a non-empty done set (e.g. re-processing or queue length checks break). findings.title: Restore numeric sort; default sort ranks scores as strings
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator stringifies elements, so scores are ordered lexicographically, not numerically, before reverse(). The cutoff at line 15 (scores[Math.min(n,len)-1]) then selects the wrong value. Example: players [{score:9},{score:10}], n=1 -> map=[9,10] -> sort() => [10,9] (string order) -> reverse() => [9,10] -> cutoff=scores[0]=9 -> filter(score>=9)=[9,10] -> slice(0,1)=[9], returning the score-9 player instead of the true top-1 (score 10). Base code used scores.sort((a,b)=>b-a) and correctly returned 10. Any multi-digit vs single-digit mix (e.g. [100,9,5]) can also shift the nth element, corrupting the top-N set and formatBoard output.

findings.title: rankScores sorts lexicographically, breaking topPlayers ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: The base used scores.sort((a, b) => b - a) (numeric descending). The new rankScores uses the default Array.prototype.sort(), which compares String(element) as UTF-16 code units, then .reverse(). For multi-digit or negative scores the result is not numerically descending, so the cutoff chosen by topPlayers (scores[Math.min(n, len)-1]) is wrong and it selects the wrong players. Example: topPlayers([{name:'a',score:9},{name:'b',score:10}], 1) -> sort() gives [10,9] ('10' < '9'), reverse gives [9,10], cutoff = 9, filter keeps both, slice(0,1) returns the score-9 player instead of the score-10 player. This is exported public API and feeds formatBoard.

findings.title: Use numeric descending comparator; default sort drops top players
findings.whyItBreaks: `scores.sort()` with no comparator coerces each number to a string and sorts by UTF-16 code units (lexicographic), not numerically; `.reverse()` then yields a descending *string* order. The cutoff at line 15 is read from that mis-ordered array, so `players.filter(p => p.score >= cutoff)` excludes valid players. Concrete: players scores [100, 10, 9], n=2 -> sort() gives ['10','100','9'] = [10,100,9], reverse -> [9,100,10], cutoff = scores[1] = 100, filter keeps only score>=100 -> [100]. findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC signature comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the sole gate for handle()'s 401/200 decision (app/webhook.py:14). Replacing hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature) with `expected == given_signature` makes the comparison short-circuit on the first differing byte, so the response time leaks how many leading hex digits of the attacker-supplied signature are correct. A network attacker can iteratively recover a valid HMAC and forge webhook payloads that handle() accepts (status 200, processor invoked), defeating the authentication this module exists to provide.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison in verify()

Replacing hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature) with the short-circuiting `==` makes comparison time depend on the position of the first differing byte, giving an attacker an oracle to recover the expected HMAC byte-by-byte and forge a valid signature. This is a regression: base compared in constant time; head does not. hmac is still imported for signature_of, so this is purely the loss of the constant-time comparison.

The new body uses `==`, which compares str/bytes with early-exit on the first mismatching byte, so comparison time depends on how many leading bytes of the attacker-supplied signature match the expected HMAC. handle() gates payload processing on verify() (app/webhook.py:14-16: returns 401 when verify is falsy, otherwise 200 and runs processor(payload)), so this timing leak lets an attacker recover a valid signature byte-by-byte and forge a webhook that is accepted and executed. findings.title: Balance updates run outside the transaction, breaking transfer atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR all three writes (ledger insert, debit, credit) ran inside `with db.transaction()` and committed or rolled back as one unit. Now only `_record_ledger` is inside the transaction (app/transfer.py:22-23) and `_apply_balances` (app/transfer.py:24) executes after it commits, so its two UPDATEs run outside any transaction and are no longer atomic even with each other. If the process crashes or either UPDATE raises after the ledger insert commits, the ledger permanently records a transfer whose balances were never applied (or only the debit was applied without the credit). That silently destroys/creates funds and corrupts account balances — exactly the partial-write failure the transaction existed to prevent. The `cents <= 0` guard does not cover this; there is no compensating rollback or error handling around the post-commit updates.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change all three statements (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) ran inside `with db.transaction():`, so any failure rolled back the whole transfer. Now only `_record_ledger` runs inside the transaction (line 23) and it commits when the `with` block exits; `_apply_balances` (line 24) runs afterwards outside any transaction. If the second UPDATE in `_apply_balances` (app/transfer.py:13-16) raises — or the process dies between the two UPDATEs — the ledger row is already committed while the debit may have persisted and the credit did not, leaving a phantom ledger entry and unbalanced/vanishing funds with no rollback. The base code (1d7649d:app/transfer.py:4-16) committed or rolled back these three writes as one unit; this PR removes that guarantee.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside the transfer transaction

The change keeps only `_record_ledger` inside the transaction and runs `_apply_balances` (the debit and credit UPDATEs) afterward, outside it. The ledger insert now commits before any balance is touched, and the two UPDATEs are themselves no longer atomic with each other. Consequences on a live path: (1) if the credit UPDATE fails after the debit UPDATE succeeded, the source account is debited with no matching credit — funds destroyed with no rollback; (2) if anything fails after the ledger commit, the ledger permanently records a transfer that never moved money (accounting divergence); (3) the debit and credit can commit independently, allowing partial transfers. The whole point of wrapping these three statements was atomicity, which this diff removes.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time, breaking timezone-stable billing days

Any billing/period grouping keyed on this value can attribute a charge to the wrong day (or a different day per host), which is exactly the non-determinism the UTC version avoided. sameBillingDay() inherits the same TZ-dependent comparison.

findings.whyItBreaks: The change drops `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64`, so spawnSync falls back to Node's 1 MiB default. git() is used to capture the full PR patch at line 140 (`git diff <mergeBase> <headSha>`), and `changedFileSet` also runs a git diff. findings.title: Restore maxBuffer so git diff does not fail on large PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: Dropping maxBuffer reverts this spawnSync to Node's default cap of 1 MiB. findings.title: Restore explicit read-only sandbox for codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `-s read-only` from the `codex exec` argument list. Previously the child codex process was unconditionally forced into the read-only sandbox (no filesystem writes, no network). Now the effective sandbox is whatever the ambient Codex config resolves to (e.g. `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` or `"danger-full-access"` in config.toml), or whatever a future CLI default becomes. Because `runCodex` feeds repository content as the prompt and runs with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (line 24), a non-read-only sandbox lets the agent write into the repo under review (or reach the network), which is exactly the least-privilege boundary this flag enforced. Dropping an explicit security constraint in a code path that executes a model over untrusted repo input is a real regression, not a style nit.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox for codex exec review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` with cwd=opts.repoPath (the repo under review) and feeds the prompt via stdin. Removing `-s read-only` means the child no longer runs under the read-only sandbox policy and instead inherits the effective sandbox mode — workspace-write by CLI default, and `danger-full-access` on this host where `~/.codex/config.toml` sets `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"`. The reviewed repo's diff, AGENTS.md and file contents are untrusted input to a code-review harness whose contract is inspection only; with write access the model can now be prompt-injected into modifying/deleting files in the reviewed workspace (or beyond it under danger-full-access) — precisely the mutation the old flag prevented. The only legitimate output path, `--output-last-message`, is written by the CLI itself, not by sandboxed shell commands, so read-only does not block it.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox on codex exec invocation
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` and feeds it the PR prompt (untrusted input derived from the code under review). The old `-s read-only` forced the reviewer into a read-only sandbox; removing it makes the sandbox mode fall back to ambient config. Codex resolves the default in `derive_permission_profile` as `configured_sandbox_mode.or_else(|| trusted/untrusted project => WorkspaceWrite).unwrap_or_default()`, so for any repo the user has trusted (the normal case for a local dev checkout) the subprocess runs `workspace-write`, which per the Codex docs lets the agent "edit within the workspace, and run routine local commands inside that boundary" without approval. If the user's config sets `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"`, the subprocess now runs unrestricted. This removes the isolation that stopped a prompt-injected/malicious PR from making the reviewing agent mutate the repo it is reviewing or execute code in it.

findings.title: Restore merge-base/headSha so patch reflects only PR changes
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code computed mergeBase = git merge-base(baseSha, headSha) and diffed mergeBase..headSha (three-dot semantics: only commits reachable from the PR head, i.e. the PR's own changes). The new code diffs baseSha..HEAD (two-dot). headSha is still read at line 137 and used as the bundle headSha (line 165) and for posting the review/check (lines 178-179), but the patch and changedFiles (line 140 -> changedFileSet -> git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD, line 57) are now generated from the local checkout's HEAD. Two concrete failures: (1) whenever PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checked-out HEAD (e.g. a workflow that checks out refs/pull/N/head or the base branch while exporting PR_HEAD_SHA), the diff/changedFiles describe a different revision than the headSha the review is attributed to, so findings and line numbers map to the wrong commit; (2) when baseSha is not an ancestor of HEAD (the normal case once main advances past the PR's branch point), the two-dot diff also contains the base-branch commits in reverse, so files changed only on main appear in the patch and in changedFiles/classifyFiles as if the PR touched them, producing false findings on unchanged code. The removed merge-base call is exactly what prevented both.

findings.title: Restore merge-base when computing PR diff and changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the patch was `git diff merge-base(baseSha, headSha) headSha` (three-dot, exactly the PR's changes) and changedFileSet was rooted at that merge base. Now it is `git diff baseSha HEAD` and `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD`. When PR_BASE_SHA is set to the base branch tip (the Actions path this adapter is written for: `GITHUB_REPOSITORY not set (must run in Actions)`) and the PR branch is behind main / main has advanced past the fork point, two-dot diff also emits the base branch's own commits as reversed changes. The model then reviews unrelated main changes, and changedPaths (used by inlineComments) is polluted with files that are not in the actual PR diff, so inline review comments can be posted against paths/lines absent from the PR (GitHub 422, then the fallback re-posts the review with no inline comments). It also stops honoring PR_HEAD_SHA for the patch, so when HEAD is the Actions merge commit the diffed tree is not necessarily the PR head.

findings.title: Restore merge-base so the diff excludes base-branch-only commits
findings.whyItBreaks: `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot comparison against the base tip, and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` (line 140) does `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` (line 57). The removed code diffed from `git merge-base baseSha headSha`. `PR_BASE_SHA` is the base branch tip, not the PR's fork point, so once base has advanced past the fork point the produced `patch` and `changedFiles` contain commits that exist only on the base branch (spurious hunks and reversed base-only changes). `changedFiles` drives `classifyFiles` (surface/policy classification at line 58) and `changedPaths` filters inline comments (lines 61-63), so the reviewer can be run against non-PR changes and inline comments can be anchored to files the PR never touched. Assumes HEAD is the PR head commit; see residual risk.

findings.title: Restore function replacers; string replacement corrupts $ patterns
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace(pat, str) treats the replacement string as a pattern template, so $$ -> $, $& -> the matched token, $` -> everything before the match, and $' -> everything after the match are re-expanded. The base code used arrow-function replacers (() => JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2), () => JSON.stringify(candidate, null, 2), () => bundle.patch) precisely to inject the values verbatim; this PR removes them, so any injected text containing those sequences is silently rewritten. bundle.patch (a raw unified diff, e.g. shell/Makefile/regex/template-literal hunks containing $$, $&, $', or $`) and JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2) output (line 25, also carries bundle.patch) now get mangled: e.g. a $& in the diff collapses to the literal '{{PATCH}}' placeholder, and $' splices the entire prompt suffix into the patch region. This is a regression introduced by this diff on the core review path.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to stop $-pattern corruption of prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: With a plain-string replacement, `String.prototype.replace` applies special replacement patterns to the replacement text: `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched placeholder, `` $` ``→everything before the match, `$'`→everything after it. `bundle.patch` is arbitrary raw diff text, so a patch containing `$$` (common in shell/Makefile/JS), `$&`, `` $` ``, or `$'` is silently rewritten before the critic model sees it (verified in V8: `'{{PATCH}}'.replace('{{PATCH}}','x$$y')` yields `x$y`; `x$&y` yields `x{{PATCH}}y`; `$'` duplicates the trailing prompt). The same corruption applies at line 25 for the bundle JSON and line 32 for the candidate JSON. The base version's `() => ...` thunks existed precisely to force verbatim insertion, so this is an introduced regression on the core review-input path.

findings.title: Use function replacer so `$` in bundle/patch is not mangled
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base, `.replace("{{BUNDLE}}", () => JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2))`, `() => JSON.stringify(candidate,...)` and `() => bundle.patch` pass a *function* replacer, whose return value is inserted literally. The head passes plain strings, so `String.prototype.replace` applies GetSubstitution to `$$`, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'` (and `$n`) found in the inserted text. `bundle.patch` is a raw diff of arbitrary code and `JSON.stringify(bundle)` is not `$`-escaped, so common source tokens are rewritten: `$$` (Makefile/shell PID, escaped template literal) becomes `$`, and `$&` (regex replacement in reviewed code) is replaced by the matched placeholder literal (`{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{PATCH}}`), while `$'`/`` $` `` splice in the template's suffix/prefix. The result is that the reviewed diff/bundle handed to `runCodex` no longer matches the actual patch, so the candidate and critic models review altered content and can produce wrong findings/verdicts with no error surfaced.

findings.title: Stop fabricating findings from malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously threw on any malformed finding (invalid/missing severity, category, file, title, whyItBreaks, suggestedFix, lineStart/lineEnd). It now silently coerces everything to a structurally valid Finding: invalid severity -> "P1", invalid category -> "bug", missing file -> "", lineStart -> 0, lineEnd -> 0, title -> "Untitled finding". The failure signal is discarded, so a caller cannot distinguish a real finding from a fabricated one and will persist/report garbage as a genuine finding. The severity default is especially dangerous: unknown severity escalates to P1 (the most blocking non-P0 level), so malformed input can force a changes_requested-style verdict. This is an exported/public swallow site, so the unusable contract is the defect regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Restore normalizeReview strict/drop contract for malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) lost its strict parameter, and line 131 now unconditionally maps every element through the non-throwing normalizeFinding. Previously strict=false callers got malformed findings filtered out (try/catch -> null -> filtered), while strict=true callers got a hard error. After this change: strict callers no longer get an error, and lenient callers no longer get dropped entries — both now receive fabricated findings; TypeScript callers passing strict will also fail to compile against the 1-arg signature. This is a public API/behavior break.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of silently defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: The base normalizeFinding threw a controlled Error for a non-object, an invalid severity/category, an empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and a non-finite or non-positive lineStart/lineEnd, and normalizeReview(strict=true) propagated it so malformed model output failed loudly. The new body keeps no guard: normalizeFinding({}) or normalizeFinding({severity:'critical', lineStart:'src/x.ts:9'}) now returns severity:'P1', title:'Untitled finding', category:'bug', file:'', lineStart:0, lineEnd:0 (Number('...') also yields NaN), i.e. a fabricated reportable finding. Because normalizeFinding is exported and normalizeReview now maps it unconditionally, every consumer is forced to conflate 'no valid finding' with a real P1 anchored at file '' line 0; the failure signal that callers previously could catch is gone. (The check also dropped the base `.trim()` on category, so a valid 'security ' is now silently recategorized to 'bug'.)

findings.title: Silently coerce malformed findings instead of rejecting them
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously threw on malformed input (not an object, invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-positive lineStart/lineEnd). It now returns a Finding for ANY input: an invalid or missing severity becomes severity "P1", an invalid/missing category becomes "bug", a missing file becomes "" and a missing/garbage lineStart becomes 0. Because normalizeReview (line 131) now always maps through this non-throwing function, the former strict path (throw) and non-strict path (drop via try/catch + null filter) are both gone: a malformed review payload yields plausible-looking, fabricated findings that are indistinguishable from genuine ones and are persisted/reported as real (a bogus "P1 bug at file "" line 0" can drive a changes_requested verdict). Failure and the fallback value can no longer be told apart.

Passing `-R "$REPO"` (as before, with REPO re-added to the step env) resolves the repository without any local clone.

Because the calls are wrapped in `echo "$(...)"`, the non-zero exit is discarded and the step still succeeds (verified with bash -e), so `steps.refs.outputs.head/base` come back empty: the workflow_dispatch path then checks out the default ref and passes empty `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` to the review instead of the requested PR. findings.title: Lenient candidate parse silently drops malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) only drops findings when strict is false: each finding is run through normalizeFinding in a try/catch and any throw (invalid/missing severity or category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-positive lineStart/lineEnd, low-confidence blocker) is mapped to null and filtered out. Passing false here silently removes a real P0/P1/P2 finding that merely has one malformed field, and the gate on line 30 only checks summary/checked, not findings, so an emptied findings list still passes. candidate.findings is the sole input handed to the critic via {{FINDINGS}} (line 35), and the critic prunes candidate findings rather than re-deriving them, so a dropped finding never reaches pruned.findings and deriveVerdict (line 43) can return pass instead of changes_requested — a false approval.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed input as an empty valid review
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw on null/non-object input, a missing/non-string summary, and missing findings/checked/residual_risks arrays (24348b3:src/shared/schema.ts:114-138). Because this is an exported function, every caller is forced to conflate 'the model produced a legitimate empty review' with 'the model output was malformed and could not be parsed' — the failure surface is reported downstream as a clean no-findings review (likely a pass/approve) with no error signal at any decision point.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently coerces malformed output to an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed guards threw on `raw == null`, non-object input, non-string `summary`, and non-array `findings`/`checked`/`residual_risks`. The failure signal is destroyed at an exported boundary, so every caller is forced to conflate 'review failed to parse' with 'review found nothing', and a parse failure that should surface (retry / needs_human / error) instead reads as a passing review.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently swallows malformed review output as empty
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change normalizeReview threw `malformed review output: ...` when raw was not an object, summary was not a string, or findings/checked/residual_risks were not arrays. The new body removes all of those throws and instead defaults: findings=[] (line 116-117), residual_risks=[] (118-123), summary=String(raw?.summary ?? "") (line 125), checked=[] (line 127). A malformed model response now returns an indistinguishable, apparently-valid RawReview with an empty summary and zero findings. The failure signal (the thrown Error) that a caller previously received to detect and retry/report bad model output is discarded, and there is no logging or other marker to tell the two cases apart. TRIGGER D: an exported public entry point that maps a failure state onto a default value.

findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is null, so github.event.pull_request.base.sha / head.sha evaluate to empty strings; the checkout ref on line 29 falls back to github.ref (the default branch, e.g. refs/heads/main) instead of the target PR head. findings.title: Don't downgrade errored-review check from failure to neutral

On GitHub a neutral check counts as a passing status for required status checks, and it is the exact conclusion used for the legitimate needs_human verdict (VERDICT_CONCLUSION.needs_human = "neutral" @src/adapters/github.ts:53). A crashed/failed review therefore (a) no longer blocks merge via the required "Needlefish" check and (b) is indistinguishable at the check-conclusion level from a real needs_human result, even though the title/summary still say the review failed and 'did NOT pass this PR'. The failure signal that previously reached the check-run consumer (branch protection / merge gate) is now conflated with a normal non-blocking verdict.

findings.title: Don't downgrade errored review check from failure to neutral

GitHub treats a neutral conclusion as successful for required status checks, so when review throws (LLM/API/gh failure) the "Needlefish" check no longer blocks the PR and can merge unreviewed, contradicting the reported summary. findings.title: Failed review posts neutral check, no longer blocking merge
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, postCheck is called with conclusion "neutral" (line 191). GitHub treats a neutral required status check as successful, so a repository that requires the Needlefish check will now allow the PR to merge even though the review errored. The unchanged summary at line 193 still claims "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR", so the tool's own contract is violated by the body. Before this change the same path posted "failure" (base a68abba src/adapters/github.ts:187), which blocked merge; the change silently turns a blocking failure into a pass, letting an attacker who can force the review to error (e.g. oversized/malformed PR) bypass review entirely.

Because the review job has `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write` (lines 17-19), a same-repo PR (the only case that reaches this job, per line 24) can modify `src/cli.ts` to emit a clean PASS / skip findings while simultaneously introducing real defects, and the concurrency is such that the untrusted PR code runs before/while the review result is posted. The review gate is therefore self-referential: the artifact being judged decides its own verdict. The reverted pattern (pinning the tool to a trusted revision such as the PR's base SHA) was the only thing preventing this.

findings.title: Severity normalization dropped; lowercase/padded severities downgrade to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: Head matched `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)` (line 97) directly, deleting the base `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and returning `raw.severity`/default `"P3"`. `normalizeReview(raw: any)` feeds unvalidated parsed JSON straight into `normalizeFinding` (src/shared/schema.ts:132), so non-canonical values are the expected input, not hypothetical. Substituting real values: raw.severity "p1" or "P0 " previously normalized to "P1"/"P0" and were preserved; now `includes("p1")`/`includes("P0 ")` is false, so they fall through to the new default "P3" (line 99). A valid P0/P1 finding emitted in lowercase or with whitespace is silently reclassified as lowest severity, hiding serious findings and never reporting the downgrade. The P1→P3 default flip compounds it but the "p1"→P3 loss is a regression independent of the default policy.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization; invalid casing now silently becomes P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The base canonicalized the value first (String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()) and consulted SEVERITIES, falling back to "P1". The new body feeds raw.severity straight into SEVERITIES.includes, so any valid-but-unnormalized value ('p1', ' P1 ', or a non-string) fails the check and is silently rewritten to the new, lowest fallback "P3". The function is exported and named normalizeFinding, so callers (normalizeReview @src/shared/schema.ts:132 passes raw LLM review JSON through untouched) trust it to canonicalize severity; instead a real P1 finding is reported as P3, under-severitizing it and (for a severity→verdict consumer outside this repo) potentially not blocking the merge it should block. Failure (unrecognized severity) is now indistinguishable from a legitimate P3.

findings.title: Restore trim/uppercase severity normalization in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code did `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` then matched `sev`. Head matches `raw.severity` directly with no trim/case-folding, so any value that previously normalized now fails `SEVERITIES.includes(...)`: substituting severity="p0" (or " p1 ") → guard `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)` @src/shared/schema.ts:97 → false → branch "P3", whereas base produced "P0". `normalizeReview` feeds raw model JSON through `raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)` @src/shared/schema.ts:132, so a genuine critical finding emitted in lowercase is silently downgraded to the lowest severity. The concurrent default change from "P1" to "P3" amplifies this: malformed/unmatched severities now land at the least-severe bucket.

findings.title: Restore stripping of GitHub tokens from codex subprocess env
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, `const env = { ...process.env }` had GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN deleted and that sanitized object was passed as the `env` option. The diff deletes both the deletions and the `env` option, so spawnSync falls back to its default of inheriting the full parent `process.env`. The spawned `codex exec` agent process (which runs model-directed commands and has network access even under `-s read-only`) now receives the caller's live GitHub credentials, enabling secret exfiltration, whereas previously those tokens were scrubbed from its environment. read-only sandboxing restricts filesystem writes, not env exposure or network egress.

findings.title: Restore stripping of GH/GITHUB tokens before spawning codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change `runCodex` built `const env = { ...process.env }`, deleted `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`, and passed `env` to `spawnSync`. With those six lines removed and no `env` option supplied, `spawnSync` defaults to inheriting the parent environment, so all three credentials are now present in the child `codex exec` process. `runCodex` feeds attacker-influenced repository/PR content into the prompt of that child, which runs with `-s read-only` but still has network access and full env visibility, so the model/agent can read and exfiltrate the operator's GitHub token. The deliberate deletion of these three variables shows the sanitization was intentional; its removal is a credential-exposure regression that re-enables secret leakage through the untrusted-content path.

findings.title: Stop leaking GitHub tokens into spawned codex process env
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted block copied process.env, removed GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN, and passed the sanitized object as spawnSync's `env`. With that gone, spawnSync falls back to its default of inheriting the full parent environment, so the codex exec child (an LLM-driven agent process, not trusted code) now receives every GitHub credential present in the runner. This reverses an explicit hardening measure: a prompt-injected or misbehaving child can read and exfiltrate the tokens that previously never crossed the process boundary. This is a credential-exposure regression introduced by this change, independent of any in-repo caller (the repo contains only this file).

findings.title: Restore fork guard: removal runs untrusted PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` from the `review` job, which previously restricted this workflow to same-repo PRs. The job runs on a `self-hosted` runner (line 18), checks out the PR head from the fork itself (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, line 23), then executes fork-controlled code: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28, runs dependency/lockfile lifecycle scripts) and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts ...` (line 34) with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` (line 33). With the guard gone, any external user can open a fork PR (`on: pull_request types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]`) and get arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted runner. GitHub downgrades the fork GITHUB_TOKEN on `pull_request`, but the runner itself (persistent state, host/network access) is exposed, which the guard existed to prevent.

findings.title: Restore fork-PR guard on self-hosted review runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The job is `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18) and the diff deletes its only gate `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository`. That predicate existed precisely to keep external fork PRs off this persistent, self-hosted machine. Without it, any outside contributor can open a PR that triggers this workflow, and the later steps then execute attacker-controlled code on the runner: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) runs the fork's package.json lifecycle/`postinstall` scripts, and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts ...` (line 34) directly runs the PR's own `src/`. That is arbitrary code execution on internal CI infrastructure (persistence, cache/workspace poisoning, network pivot). The `pull_request` event (not `pull_request_target`) limits the GITHUB_TOKEN to read-only and withholds secrets for forks, which is why this is a runner-compromise risk rather than a direct secret exfiltration; the malicious code is invited to run, not merely able to read a token.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard before running PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control preventing PRs from forked repositories from running this job. With it removed, a fork PR (trigger `pull_request`, line 8) reaches `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18) and executes attacker-controlled code: `actions/checkout` with `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` (lines 21-23) checks out the fork commit, then `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28, which runs package lifecycle scripts from the fork) and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) run that code on a persistent self-hosted runner. GitHub explicitly warns against self-hosted runners for repos that accept fork PRs; while `pull_request` does not expose `secrets`, arbitrary code on the runner can compromise the host and any local state/credentials, enabling lateral movement.

findings.title: Honor explicit 0 grace instead of silently falling back
findings.whyItBreaks: The only behavioral change of `parsed >= 0` -> `parsed > 0` is for the value 0. 0 is a legitimate duration here: it means `setTimeout(..., 0)`, i.e. escalate SIGTERM->SIGKILL immediately (line 124) and give up immediately after SIGKILL (line 123). With this change, an operator setting NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 has their explicit value silently discarded and replaced by the defaults 5000ms (line 5) and 2000ms (line 9). The escalation that used to complete near-instantly now lingers ~7s before finish(null,'SIGKILL') runs, which can push the runner past an outer caller's deadline. Positive values and negatives behave as before, so this is a pure regression for the zero configuration.

findings.title: Zero-duration env config now silently replaced by fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: Substituting the config value "0" into the changed guard: `Number.isFinite(0) && 0 > 0` is false, so the function returns `fallbackMs` instead of 0. Before this diff `0` was accepted. Both consumers are affected: `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` (operator intent: SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM, no grace window) now produces `RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS = 5000` (line 5) and delays the SIGKILL by 5s at line 124; `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` (intent: stop waiting for child `close` immediately — the stated goal in the comment at lines 120-121) now produces `RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS = 2000` (line 9) and blocks the resolved promise an extra 2s at line 123. `0` is a valid `setTimeout` delay and nothing in the repo (no docs, no test, no validation) declares 0 invalid, so an existing deployment that sets either variable to 0 changes behavior silently on upgrade.

findings.title: Rejecting 0 silently overrides explicit timeout-grace config
findings.whyItBreaks: `readRunnerDurationMs` is a duration reader and 0 is a valid duration ("no grace / escalate immediately"). Changing `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0` makes "0" fall to `fallbackMs`, so NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 now yields 5000 (src/shared/runner-process.ts:3-5 → used at :124) and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now yields 2000 (src/shared/runner-process.ts:7-9 → used at :123). A user who deliberately configured 0 gets the default instead, with no error or warning, so the configured escalation timing is silently ignored.

findings.title: Restore deep-pass residual risks in large review
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change every deep pass's res.residual_risks (which may carry blocks:true) was accumulated and forwarded as candidateMerged.residual_risks. Now the loop drops them and line 113 hard-codes residual_risks: []. The critic at line 116 therefore never sees them, so pruned.residual_risks at line 122/128 cannot contain them, and deriveVerdict(findings, residual_risks) flips a hotspot whose evidence gap should have produced "needs_human" to "pass". A blocking uncertainty signal is silently lost on the large-PR path.

findings.title: Restore base/head SHA substitution in critic prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: critic.md promises the critic receives the base/head SHAs (its preamble says so and its footer is `Refs BASE: {{BASE}}` / `HEAD: {{HEAD}}`) so it can re-read hunks with `git diff <base>..<head>`. This diff removed `.replace("{{BASE}}", ...)`/`.replace("{{HEAD}}", ...)` from both the reviewLarge critic prompt (here) and the reviewSmall one (line 61), so the rendered prompt now contains the literal strings `{{BASE}}`/`{{HEAD}}`. On the large-PR path the critic gets only patchStat, and with unresolvable SHAs it can no longer inspect the actual diff before pruning.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop for changed files outside hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge now deep-reviews only `hotspots` (at most MAX_HOTSPOTS=6, risk-ranked). The removed backstop was the only code path that appended changed files the map pass failed to assign to a surface, preserving the stated invariant "never silently skip a changed file". With it gone, any changed file the map LLM omits is never deep-reviewed and never surfaces in checked/residual risks, so a PR can be approved while part of its diff was never examined.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so unmapped changed files are still deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge only deep-reviews files that the map pass placed inside the top-6 hotspots (`hotspots = sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)`). The deleted block computed `covered` from the selected hotspots and pushed a `tail-coverage` hotspot for every `bundle.changedFiles` path that was not covered, with the explicit comment 'never silently skip a changed file'. With that removed, any changed file absent from the map pass (or in hotspots dropped by the `slice(0, 6)`) receives no deep review and no residual-risk entry, so the tool can return a PASS verdict for files it never examined.

findings.title: Do not discard deep-pass residual risks before the critic/verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: The deep loop no longer collects `res.residual_risks` (the `residuals` array and `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` were removed), and `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is now hardcoded to `[]`. Each deep pass can emit blocking residual risks, which previously flowed into the critic payload via candidateMerged and onward to `deriveVerdict`. Now that failure/uncertainty signal is mapped to an empty value and discarded; a deep pass that could not conclude (blocks=true) no longer reaches the critic or the final `residualRisks` (which uses `pruned.residual_risks`), so the verdict can pass on a PR the deep pass flagged.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so no changed file is silently skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge keeps only sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) and no longer adds a tail hotspot for changed files not present in a selected hotspot. Any large PR (>30000 patch chars or >10 files) whose map pass emits a file outside the top-6 ranked hotspots, or files dropped by the slice, is now iterated neither in the deep loop nor flagged anywhere (residual_risks is hardcoded []), so a real bug in that file yields no finding and the review can return PASS. The deleted comment explicitly promised 'never silently skip a changed file'.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual_risks are discarded instead of propagated
findings.whyItBreaks: Base collected each deep pass's residual risks (residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)) and forwarded them in candidateMerged to the critic; the head hardcodes residual_risks: [] and no longer reads res.residual_risks at all. A deep pass that reports a blocking residual (e.g. insufficient evidence on a material issue) therefore has that signal dropped before the critic and before deriveVerdict (line 122), so the final verdict can be computed as a pass even though the deep pass flagged a blocker.

findings.title: Large-PR path silently drops caller-supplied focus/deep inputs
findings.whyItBreaks: Base forwarded `focus: bundle.focus` and `deep: bundle.deep` into `mapBundle` (base src/core/review.ts:90-91) and substituted `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` into the deep prompt (base line 117). This diff removes all three, so on the large path `bundle.focus`/`bundle.deep` are never passed to `map.md` or `deep.md`. The fields are still first-class inputs: `focus` and `deep` are part of `Bundle` and the small path still hands the whole `bundle` (including `focus`) to the model via `JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)` (src/core/review.ts:51-55). Result: identical caller input produces different reviewer behavior depending only on PR size — e.g. `focus: "auth"` is honored for a small PR but silently ignored for a large PR, and the promised `{{FOCUS}}` slot in the deep prompt is left unfilled. Silent divergence on a user/harness-supplied input is a regression, not a no-op cleanup.

findings.title: Large-review path silently ignores bundle.focus/deep
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `focus: bundle.focus` and `deep: bundle.deep` from mapBundle (head src/core/review.ts:83-89) and removes `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` from the deep prompt (head src/core/review.ts:117-121). After this change `rg -n focus src/core/review.ts` returns nothing, so on the reviewLarge path the caller-supplied focus is never passed to either the map or deep prompt. reviewSmall still serializes the whole bundle (including focus) into review.md, so focus is honored for small PRs but silently discarded for large PRs — a focus-scoped request produces an unfocused review with no signal that the directive was dropped.

findings.title: Restore the {{FOCUS}} substitution dropped from the deep prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version of this same block did `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` on deep.md (git show ddca8aa:src/core/review.ts line 122), which only existed because prompts/deep.md contains a `{{FOCUS}}` placeholder. After this diff the deep prompt is built without filling that placeholder, so (a) the literal string `{{FOCUS}}` is handed to the model instead of the user's focus text and (b) the `focus` directive is silently ignored for every large PR. The small-PR path still passes the entire bundle (including focus and deep) into review.md via JSON.stringify, so the feature still works for small PRs and the inconsistency is not a global removal. The related deletion of `focus: bundle.focus` / `deep: bundle.deep` from mapBundle (head lines 83-89) removes these fields from the map pass as well.

findings.title: Fix minutes/seconds carry so durations never render as "Xm 60s"
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code computes minutes from the raw ms and seconds independently: minutes = floor(ms/60000) and seconds = round((ms%60000)/1000). When the remainder rounds up to 60 (any ms in [k*60000+59500, k*60000+59999] for k>=1), seconds becomes 60 and is printed without carrying into minutes, producing strings like "1m 60s" for ms=119500..119999. The previous version rounded to total seconds first, so the carry happened correctly (119999 -> "2m 0s").

findings.title: formatDuration can emit 60 in the seconds field
findings.whyItBreaks: Rounding the minute remainder independently lets the seconds field reach 60, which is never a valid minute:second rendering. For ms=119600, minutes=Math.floor(119600/60000)=1 and seconds=Math.round(59600/1000)=60, so the output is "1m 60s" (the base code returned "2m 0s", since totalSeconds%60 is always 0..59). Any duration whose ms%60000>=59500 is affected. This changed string is embedded in user-facing markdown at src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80.

findings.title: formatDuration can render 60 seconds ("1m 60s"/"60s")
findings.whyItBreaks: Head computes minutes from an unrounded ms and rounds the remainder seconds independently, so the seconds component can round up to 60 without carrying into minutes. ms=119500 → minutes=floor(1.9917)=1, seconds=round(59500/1000)=60 → "1m 60s" (should be "2m 0s"); ms=59999 → "60s" (should be "1m 0s"). The base version rounded totalSeconds first (round(ms/1000)) and derived minutes/remainder from it, which never produced a 60s component, so this is a regression from the prior behavior. Output is user-visible in renderMarkdown's call-stats/total line (src/shared/render.ts:75,80).

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, contradicts its contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Relaxing `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` lets `0` pass validation. The function name (`parsePositiveInteger`) and its unchanged error message `${label} requires a positive integer` both promise a value strictly greater than zero; 0 is not a positive integer. This is an exported (public) helper, so the promised validation is the contract: callers using the result as a divisor, array size, retry/concurrency count, timeout multiplier, or other >0-requiring quantity now silently receive 0 instead of a thrown error, enabling division-by-zero, empty-loop, or off-by-one failures at a distance. The body no longer implements the promise carried by the name and error text.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 despite promising a positive integer
findings.whyItBreaks: The export's name (`parsePositiveInteger`) and its error text `${label} requires a positive integer` (src/shared/runner.ts:33) both promise the returned value is > 0, i.e. a validation guarantee. Changing the guard from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes `parsePositiveInteger('0', label)` return 0 instead of throwing, so any caller that trusts the promised positivity (e.g. a count, retry/attempt count, or `timeoutMs`) silently receives a non-positive value it believes is validated positive. The carrier was not updated to match the body, so promise != implementation; the value 0 is externally observable as a 'positive integer' result.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0 despite positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was relaxed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `parsePositiveInteger("0", ...)` now returns 0 instead of throwing. The exported symbol name and the thrown message (`${label} requires a positive integer`) promise strict positivity, so every consumer that trusts the promise (e.g. using the result as a timeoutMs, attempts, batch size, or count) silently receives an invalid zero and can hit a no-op/infinite/never-timeout path instead of failing fast on the bad input. Being an exported public validator, the contract itself is the defect even with no in-repo caller yet. Zero is not a positive integer.
